name: Security analysis of a custom hash-function construction
theory_paragraphs: A \term{cryptographic hash function} is a mathematical recipe $H$ that takes an input of ANY length (a password, a file, a whole disk image) and produces a fixed-length output of $n$ bits, called the \term{digest} or \q{fingerprint}: $H : \{0,1\}^{*} \rightarrow \{0,1\}^{n}$. Two everyday facts first: (1) $H$ is \imp{deterministic} -- hashing the same input twice always gives the same digest; (2) $H$ must be \imp{fast to compute}, because systems hash gigabytes routinely. Now the crucial observation: there are infinitely many possible inputs but only $2^{n}$ possible digests, so by the \term{pigeonhole principle} (more pigeons than holes forces two pigeons to share a hole) collisions -- two different inputs with the same digest -- are GUARANTEED to exist. Security can therefore never mean \q{collisions do not exist}; it can only mean \imp{collisions cannot be found in practice}. Every requirement below is a statement about what an attacker with realistic computing power cannot do.

The three security requirements are best learned as three GAMES between a challenger and an attacker -- what changes from game to game is only \imp{who gets to choose the inputs}:\begin{tightitem}\item \term{One-wayness (preimage resistance)}: the challenger hands the attacker a digest $h$. The attacker must find ANY input $x$ with $H(x) = h$. If this is infeasible, $H$ is one-way. (This is what protects stored password hashes: seeing $h$ should not reveal a working $x$.)\item \term{Weak collision resistance (second-preimage resistance)}: the challenger hands the attacker a concrete input $x$. The attacker must find a DIFFERENT input $y \neq x$ with $H(y) = H(x)$. (This is what protects a signed file: given the legit file, nobody should be able to craft an evil file with the same digest.)\item \term{Strong collision resistance}: the attacker chooses BOTH inputs freely. They win if they find any pair $x \neq y$ with $H(x) = H(y)$.\end{tightitem}Because the strong game gives the attacker the most freedom, it is the EASIEST game for the attacker to win. Consequence to memorize: \imp{strong collision resistance implies weak collision resistance}. Indeed, if an attacker could win the weak game (break $H$ for a given $x$), the same trick wins the strong game (just ignore the freedom to pick $x$). Equivalently: once you disprove strong collision resistance, check whether the same trick still works when $x$ is fixed -- it usually does, and then weak is broken too.

Two ingredients appear in every exam construction, so learn them from zero. First, \term{bitwise xor}, written $\oplus$: it compares two bits and outputs $1$ exactly when they differ ($0 \oplus 0 = 0$, $0 \oplus 1 = 1$, $1 \oplus 0 = 1$, $1 \oplus 1 = 0$); on bit-strings it is applied position by position. Its three laws drive almost every attack:\begin{tightitem}\item self-cancellation: $b \oplus b = 0$ (any string xored with itself vanishes),\item identity: $b \oplus 0 = b$ (xoring with zeros changes nothing),\item commutativity/associativity: order does not matter, so $x_1 \oplus x_2 = x_2 \oplus x_1$.\end{tightitem}Second, \term{arithmetic modulo} $2^{n}$: integers are added/multiplied as usual but the result \q{wraps around} so only the remainder after division by $2^{n}$ is kept -- exactly like a clock with $2^{n}$ hours, so the result always fits in $n$ bits. A third useful notion is the \term{modular inverse} of a number $a$ modulo $2^{n}$: a number $a^{-1}$ with the property $a \cdot a^{-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{2^{n}}$ -- multiplying by $a^{-1}$ is the modular analogue of dividing by $a$, and it lets you undo a multiplication. Such an inverse exists precisely when $a$ is ODD; for small cases you can find it by trial: e.g. $3^{-1} \equiv 171 \pmod{2^{8}}$ because $3 \cdot 171 = 513 = 2 \cdot 256 + 1 \equiv 1 \pmod{256}$. Key fact used in attacks: an equation $a \cdot z \equiv c \pmod{2^{n}}$ can be solved for $z$ precisely when $a$ is ODD, because only then does the modular inverse $a^{-1} \bmod 2^{n}$ exist; then $z \equiv a^{-1} \cdot c \pmod{2^{n}}$.

Exam constructions always split a candidate hash into a \term{secure primitive} $P$ -- a building block you are TOLD to assume is secure (SHA256 / SHA-2, sometimes AES) -- and a \term{combiner} $C$, some extra plumbing (xor of blocks, a weighted sum, dropped blocks, appended input bits). Classify the shape before analyzing:\begin{tightitem}\item \term{Combiner inside the primitive}: $H(x) = P(C(x))$, e.g. $H(x) = \mathrm{SHA256}(x_1 \oplus \cdots \oplus x_n)$. The attacker never touches $P$ directly, but fully controls what goes INTO it via $C$. If $C$ is linear (xor, sums mod $2^{n}$), its cancellation laws let the attacker manufacture different inputs with the SAME combiner value, hence the same digest: the collision properties typically FAIL. One-wayness usually survives, because winning the one-way game still forces the attacker to invert $P$ on some point.\item \term{Combiner outside the primitive}: $H(x) = P(x) \,\|\, C(x)$ (the symbol $\|$ is \term{concatenation}: writing two bit-strings one after another). Example: append the last 128 input bits to the SHA256 output -- written $LSB_{128}(x)$, where $LSB_{k}(x)$ denotes the \term{least significant bits} of $x$, i.e. its LAST $k$ bits (the rightmost bits when $x$ is written as a bit-string). Now the primitive's output sits verbatim inside the digest, so $H(x) = H(y)$ forces $P(x) = P(y)$: every property of $P$ transfers to $H$, and all three requirements typically HOLD -- but the construction is \imp{never stronger than its primitive part}, since only the $P$-bits of the digest do security work.\end{tightitem}

Two proof techniques settle every sub-question, and both are simpler than they sound. \term{Disproof by construction} (used to show a property FAILS): you must EXHIBIT a concrete winning move -- an actual preimage or an actual colliding pair -- and verify it by plugging it into the formula. With a linear combiner this is pure algebra: permute blocks (commutativity), duplicate a block twice (self-cancellation), append an all-zero block (adds nothing), or solve one modular equation for one block of $y$ while keeping the combiner value fixed. \term{Proof by reduction} (used to show a property HOLDS): you argue by contradiction. Assume some adversary $\mathcal{A}$ could break the property for $H$; then show that the same $\mathcal{A}$, with a little repackaging, also breaks the corresponding property of the primitive $P$. Since $P$ was assumed secure, the assumption must be false, so the property holds for $H$. Example: if $H(x) = \mathrm{SHA256}(x) \,\|\, C(x)$ and an adversary finds $x \neq y$ with $H(x) = H(y)$, then in particular the SHA256 halves are equal, i.e. $(x,y)$ is a collision for SHA256 -- contradiction. \imp{A disproof needs a concrete counterexample; a proof needs a reduction to the primitive} -- never mix the two up.

One final exam signal: when the problem remarks that a block cipher's encryption $E_K$ and decryption $D_K$ are \imp{mutual inverses} and the key is known, it is telling you that YOU may apply $D_K$ freely when building attacks. A block cipher with a known key gives no one-wayness at all -- it is a reversible scrambling, not a one-way function -- so reductions to \q{security of the primitive} collapse and preimages can be built by decrypting the target digest and then fixing up the combiner. Watch for this remark; it flips the expected verdicts.
theory_cheatsheet: One-way: given digest $h$, finding any $x$ with $H(x)=h$ must be infeasible (attacker picks $x$).
Weak collision: given $x$, finding $y \neq x$ with $H(y)=H(x)$ must be infeasible (challenger fixes $x$).
Strong collision: finding ANY pair $x \neq y$ with $H(x)=H(y)$ must be infeasible (easiest attacker game).
Strong collision resistance $\Rightarrow$ weak collision resistance; after breaking strong, re-check the trick with $x$ fixed.
Xor laws: $b \oplus b = 0$, $b \oplus 0 = b$, commutative $\Rightarrow$ permuted or twice-duplicated blocks collide; $a \cdot z \equiv c \pmod{2^n}$ solvable iff $a$ odd.
Disproof = exhibit a concrete pair/preimage and verify; proof = reduction: breaking $H$ would break the assumed-secure primitive $P$.
identify_givens: A concrete hash $H$ built from a stated secure primitive (SHA256/SHA-2, sometimes AES with the remark that encrypt/decrypt are mutual inverses) plus a combiner: bitwise xor of input blocks, weighted sums $\bmod\, 2^n$, dropping/duplicating blocks, or concatenating input bits (e.g. $LSB_{128}(x)$) to the primitive's output. Often given as short pseudocode like `def hash(x): H = SHA256(x); H = H ++ LSB128(x); return H` or a formula $H(x) = \mathrm{SHA}(x_1 \oplus \cdots \oplus x_n)$ over blocks of 256 bits.
identify_target: For EACH of the three requirements of a cryptographically secure hash function -- one-wayness (preimage resistance), weak collision resistance (second-preimage resistance), strong collision resistance -- (1) state the formal definition and (2) either disprove it by exhibiting an explicit preimage/collision or argue it holds, usually by a reduction showing an attack on $H$ implies an attack on the underlying primitive.
identify_keywords: disprove the requirement or argue why the requirement is met
strategy_name: Define all three properties, then break via combiner cancellation or prove by reduction to the primitive

algorithm.detail: Write out all three definitions BEFORE any analysis:\begin{tightitem}\item One-wayness: given $h$, infeasible to find $x$ with $H(x) = h$.\item Weak collision resistance: given $x$, infeasible to find $y \neq x$ with $H(x) = H(y)$.\item Strong collision resistance: infeasible to find any $x \neq y$ with $H(x) = H(y)$.\end{tightitem}\imp{Strong collision resistance implies weak collision resistance} -- keep this in mind when ordering your verdicts.

Split $H$ into the secure primitive $P$ (SHA256/AES) and the combiner $C$, and classify the shape:\begin{tightitem}\item \term{Combiner inside}: $H(x) = P(C(x))$ -- cancellation attacks on $C$ become possible; expect broken collision properties.\item \term{Combiner outside}: $H(x) = P(x) \,\|\, C(x)$ -- $P$'s output appears verbatim in the digest; expect reductions, not breaks.\item \term{No primitive at all}: $H$ is a pure linear combiner (e.g. $H = \sum_i i \cdot x_i \bmod 2^{128}$); then ALL THREE properties are directly attackable by algebra.\end{tightitem}

This is the attacker's easiest game (both inputs free). Exploit linearity/cancellation of $C$:\begin{tightitem}\item Xor combiner: permute the blocks ($H(x_1 \| x_2) = H(x_2 \| x_1)$), duplicate a block twice ($b \oplus b = 0$), or append a zero block.\item Weighted sum $\sum_i a_i x_i \bmod 2^n$: fix all blocks of $y$ except one and solve $a_j y_j \equiv C(x) - \sum_{i \neq j} a_i y_i \pmod{2^n}$ (choose $j$ with $a_j$ odd so the inverse exists).\end{tightitem}Exhibit the pair $(x, y)$ concretely and verify both hashes match.

Now $x$ is FIXED by the challenger. Ask: does the step-3 trick still work when one input is given?\begin{tightitem}\item Usually yes: e.g. for xor, append two equal extra blocks to the fixed $x$; for a weighted sum, append a zero block ($y = (x_1, \dots, x_n, 0)$) or re-solve the modular equation for one block of $y$ keeping the same value $C(x)$.\item If the strong-collision attack needed control of BOTH inputs, weak collision resistance may survive -- argue by reduction instead.\end{tightitem}

Check three cases:\begin{tightitem}\item No secure primitive / pure combiner: solve the linear equation directly (e.g. for $H = \sum_i i \cdot x_i \bmod 2^{128}$, the single block $x_1 = h$ gives $H(x) = h$) -- BROKEN.\item Block cipher with known key: apply $D_K$ to $h$ and build a preimage via the combiner -- BROKEN.\item Secure one-way primitive $P$ present: give the reduction. Any $x$ with $H(x)=h$ yields a preimage of $P$ on some point (e.g. on $C(x)$), so one-wayness of $P$ implies one-wayness of $H$ -- HOLDS. Mention explicitly if leaked input bits (appended $LSB_{128}(x)$) do NOT by themselves invert the primitive.\end{tightitem}

algorithm.action: Argue the surviving properties and grade the strength
algorithm.detail: For each property that holds, state the reduction cleanly: an adversary breaking the property for $H$ produces a collision/preimage for $P$ (e.g. $H(x)=H(y)$ with the combiner outside forces $\mathrm{SHA256}(x)=\mathrm{SHA256}(y)$). Close with a strength note if applicable: \imp{a construction is never stronger than its primitive part} -- e.g. only 256 of 384 output bits come from SHA256, so the effective security is that of the 256-bit part.

variations.name: Xor combiner inside the primitive
variations.detail: E.g. $H(x) = \mathrm{SHA256}(x_1 \oplus \cdots \oplus x_n)$ over 256-bit blocks. Strong collision resistance FAILS: any permutation of the blocks, or a block duplicated twice, gives the same xor and hence the same digest -- exhibit $H(x_1 \| x_2) = H(x_2 \| x_1)$. Weak collision resistance fails by appending two equal blocks to the fixed $x$ ($b \oplus b = 0$). One-wayness HOLDS by reduction: a preimage of $H$ still requires inverting SHA256 on some input.

variations.name: Combiner outside via concatenation (all properties hold, but weakened)
variations.detail: E.g. $H(x) = \mathrm{SHA256}(x) \,\|\, LSB_{128}(x)$. Trap: the appended plaintext bits LOOK like a leak, but they do not help invert the SHA256 half. All three properties HOLD by reduction -- a collision or preimage for $H$ forces one for SHA256 -- but the construction is strictly weaker than plain SHA256 since security rests only on the 256-bit part while the output is 384 bits. \imp{Do not claim this construction is broken}; the expected verdict is \q{met, but weaker}.

variations.name: Modular/weighted-sum combiner, possibly with NO primitive
variations.detail: Combiner $C(x) = \sum_i a_i x_i \bmod 2^n$ or a polynomial rolling hash, sometimes without any secure primitive around it. Collisions are linear algebra mod $2^n$: fix all blocks of $y$ but one and solve $a_j y_j \equiv C(x) - \sum_{i \neq j} a_i y_i \pmod{2^n}$. If there is no primitive, even ONE-WAYNESS falls: for $H = \sum_i i \cdot x_i \bmod 2^{128}$ the single block $x_1 = h$ is a preimage. Traps:\begin{tightitem}\item If $a_j$ is even it has no inverse $\bmod\, 2^n$ -- pick a block with odd coefficient (the index $1$ is always odd and always available).\item Forgetting the modulus, or dividing instead of multiplying by the modular inverse.\end{tightitem}

variations.name: Encrypt/decrypt mutual-inverse remark
variations.detail: When the problem remarks that $E_K$ and $D_K$ are mutual inverses, it signals that you may APPLY $D_K$ when constructing preimages/collisions: the block cipher is NOT one-way for an attacker who knows $K$. Invert the cipher freely -- only the combiner constrains you -- and note that reductions to \q{security of the primitive} then fail.

walkthrough_problem:
A software vendor fingerprints download files as follows. The file $x$ is split into 256-bit blocks $x_1, \dots, x_n$ (the last block is zero-padded), interpreted as integers, and the fingerprint is computed as
\[ H(x) \;=\; \mathrm{SHA256}\Big( \big(x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n\big) \bmod 2^{256} \Big), \]
where SHA256 is the (assumed secure) SHA-2 hash with 256-bit output. For each of the three requirements of a cryptographically secure hash function (one-wayness, weak collision resistance, strong collision resistance): define the requirement, and either disprove the requirement or argue why the requirement is met.

walkthrough_steps.work: Write the three definitions first -- the exam always asks for them, and writing them down tells you exactly which game you must win or lose in each part. \term{One-wayness}: given a digest $h$ it is infeasible to find any $x$ with $H(x) = h$. \term{Weak collision resistance}: given a fixed $x$ it is infeasible to find $y \neq x$ with $H(x) = H(y)$. \term{Strong collision resistance}: it is infeasible to find ANY pair $x \neq y$ with $H(x) = H(y)$. Beginner tip: keep track of WHO chooses the inputs -- attacker-free-choice (one-way, strong) versus challenger-fixed-$x$ (weak). A common mistake is to \q{disprove} weak collision resistance with a pair where you chose $x$ yourself; that only disproves the strong version.

Decompose before attacking. Here $H = P \circ C$ with primitive $P = \mathrm{SHA256}$ and combiner $C(x) = \big(\sum_i x_i\big) \bmod 2^{256}$ sitting INSIDE the primitive's input. Why this matters: you never attack SHA256; you attack what gets FED into it. Addition mod $2^{256}$ is linear and commutative, so many different block arrangements share the same sum -- and everything with the same sum gets the same digest. Prediction (which you now confirm): collision properties broken, one-wayness probably intact. Beginners often skip this prediction step and then waste time trying to \q{break SHA256} -- you never need to.

Strong collision resistance -- BROKEN. You control both inputs, so pick the simplest possible pair that keeps the sum fixed. Take $a = 1$ and $b = 2$ (as 256-bit integers) and set $x = a \| b$ (two blocks) and $y = b \| a$. Addition is commutative, so $C(x) = (1+2) \bmod 2^{256} = 3 = C(y)$, hence
\[ H(x) = \mathrm{SHA256}(3) = H(y), \]
an explicit collision with $x \neq y$. An even simpler pair: the one-block input $x = 5$ versus the two-block input $y = 2 \| 3$, both with sum $5$. Mistake to avoid: it is not enough to SAY \q{sums collide}; you must write down a concrete pair and verify both sides evaluate to the same digest.

Weak collision resistance -- BROKEN. Now $x = x_1 \| \cdots \| x_n$ is handed to you, fixed. The trick from Step 3 must be adapted so that it works for THIS $x$: compute the target sum $S = \big(\sum_i x_i\big) \bmod 2^{256}$ and build any $y$ with the same sum. Take $y = y_1 \| y_2$ with $y_1$ arbitrary and $y_2 = (S - y_1) \bmod 2^{256}$; then $C(y) = (y_1 + y_2) \bmod 2^{256} = S = C(x)$, so $H(y) = H(x)$. Concrete numbers: if $x = 7 \| 9$ then $S = 16$; choose $y_1 = 4$, $y_2 = (16 - 4) \bmod 2^{256} = 12$; check: $H(y) = \mathrm{SHA256}(16) = H(x)$. Edge case a careful answer mentions: with negligible probability $2^{-256}$ your $y$ equals $x$ -- then just pick another $y_1$. The subtraction always works because every integer $v$ has an \term{additive inverse} mod $2^{256}$: the value $(2^{256} - v) \bmod 2^{256}$, which added to $v$ gives $0$ -- so $y_2 = (S - y_1) \bmod 2^{256}$ exists for every $y_1$, unlike the multiplicative case where an inverse exists only for odd coefficients.

One-wayness -- HOLDS, by reduction. Reason by contradiction: suppose an adversary, given $h$, could find $x$ with $H(x) = h$. By definition of $H$ this means $\mathrm{SHA256}\big(C(x)\big) = h$. But then the 256-bit value $z = C(x)$ is a preimage of $h$ under SHA256 -- the adversary has inverted SHA256, which was assumed infeasible. Contradiction, so $H$ is one-way. The subtle point beginners miss: it does NOT matter that the adversary controls $z$ only indirectly through the sum; ANY preimage of $H$ whatsoever hands you SOME preimage of SHA256, and that is all the reduction needs. Also note the asymmetry with Steps 3-4: linearity lets you manufacture collisions (same sum), but it does not help you hit a prescribed digest $h$.

Conclusion and security interpretation. Strong and weak collision resistance FAIL (explicit collisions via the linear combiner); one-wayness HOLDS by reduction to SHA256. Interpretation, which exams reward: $H$ is unsuitable for fingerprinting downloads, because a malicious mirror can reorder file blocks or rebalance two blocks while preserving their sum -- the fingerprint does not change, so the integrity check is fooled -- even though inverting the fingerprint remains as hard as inverting SHA256. Collision resistance, not one-wayness, is what fingerprinting actually needs.

exam_questions.problem:
Let $x$ be an input of $n$ bits. Let $\mathrm{hash}(x)$ be the following function:
\[ \text{def } \mathrm{hash}(x):\quad H = \mathrm{SHA256}(x);\quad H = H \mathbin{++} LSB_{128}(x);\quad \text{return } H \]
Here, SHA256 is SHA-2 with 256-bit output, $LSB_{128}$ returns the last 128 bits of $x$, and $\mathbin{++}$ is bit concatenation. For each requirement of a cryptographically secure hash function, define the requirement, and either disprove the requirement or argue why the requirement is met.

solution_steps.work: Definitions. \term{One-wayness}: given $h$ it should be infeasible to find $x$ with $H(x) = h$. \term{Weak collision resistance}: given $x$ it should be infeasible to find a different $y \neq x$ with $H(x) = H(y)$. \term{Strong collision resistance}: it should be infeasible to find any pair $x \neq y$ with $H(x) = H(y)$.

Decompose: the primitive is $P = \mathrm{SHA256}$ and the combiner sits OUTSIDE: $H(x) = \mathrm{SHA256}(x) \,\|\, LSB_{128}(x)$, a 384-bit digest whose first 256 bits are the raw SHA256 output and whose last 128 bits are copied straight from the input. Shape verdict: expect reductions (all properties hold), not breaks -- the appended bits look like a leak but they are input bits, not digest bits.

One-wayness -- HOLDS (official answer: \q{it is one way, even if weaker than SHA}). If an adversary given $h$ finds $x$ with $H(x) = h$, then the first 256 bits of $h$ equal $\mathrm{SHA256}(x)$, i.e. the adversary inverted SHA256 -- contradiction with the assumed one-wayness of SHA256. Note the leak: the last 128 bits of $h$ reveal the last 128 bits of $x$, but knowing a SUFFIX of one preimage does not help FIND a preimage, and the effective security rests only on the 256-bit SHA256 part.

Weak collision resistance -- HOLDS. Given $x$, suppose an adversary finds $y \neq x$ with $H(y) = H(x)$. Comparing the first 256 digest bits gives $\mathrm{SHA256}(y) = \mathrm{SHA256}(x)$, a second preimage for SHA256 -- contradicting its assumed weak collision resistance. (Official solution: \q{if one can find $y$, then $\mathrm{SHA256}(x) = \mathrm{SHA256}(y)$}.)

Strong collision resistance -- HOLDS. Suppose an adversary finds any $x \neq y$ with $H(x) = H(y)$. Again the first 256 bits force $\mathrm{SHA256}(x) = \mathrm{SHA256}(y)$, a collision for SHA256 -- contradiction. (Official solution: \q{if one can find such pair, $\mathrm{SHA256}(x) = \mathrm{SHA256}(y)$}.)

exam_questions.answer: All three requirements are met by reduction to SHA256 (equal digests force equal SHA256 halves), but the construction is weaker than plain SHA256 since security rests only on its 256-bit part.

exam_questions.source: Exam 2020-01-10 (dasak19), Part II, Problem 3 (A level, 5 points)
exam_questions.problem: Let $x = x_1 \dots x_n$ be an input of $n$ blocks of 256 bits. Let $H(x) = \mathrm{SHA}(x_1 \oplus \cdots \oplus x_n)$, where $\oplus$ is bitwise xor and SHA is the Secure Hash Algorithm 2. Is $H$ a secure hash function? For each requirement of secure hash functions, disprove the requirement or argue why the requirement is met.

solution_steps.work: Definitions. \term{One-wayness}: given $h$, infeasible to find $x$ with $H(x) = h$. \term{Weak collision resistance}: given $x$, infeasible to find $y \neq x$ with $H(x) = H(y)$. \term{Strong collision resistance}: infeasible to find any $x \neq y$ with $H(x) = H(y)$.

Decompose: primitive $P = \mathrm{SHA\text{-}2}$, combiner $C(x) = x_1 \oplus \cdots \oplus x_n$ INSIDE the primitive. Xor is commutative, associative and self-cancelling ($b \oplus b = 0$), so different block arrangements collapse to the same 256-bit value -- expect both collision properties to fail and one-wayness to survive.

Strong collision resistance -- BROKEN (official solution). Take any two distinct 256-bit blocks $x_1 \neq x_2$ and compare the two-block inputs $x = x_1 \| x_2$ and $y = x_2 \| x_1$. Since xor is commutative, $x_1 \oplus x_2 = x_2 \oplus x_1$, hence
\[ H(x) = \mathrm{SHA}(x_1 \oplus x_2) = \mathrm{SHA}(x_2 \oplus x_1) = H(y), \]
an explicit collision.

Weak collision resistance -- BROKEN. Now $x = x_1 \| \cdots \| x_n$ is fixed. Append any block $b$ TWICE: $y = x_1 \| \cdots \| x_n \| b \| b$. Because $b \oplus b = 0$, the xor is unchanged: $C(y) = x_1 \oplus \cdots \oplus x_n \oplus b \oplus b = C(x)$, so $H(y) = H(x)$ with $y \neq x$. (Alternatively, swap any two blocks of the fixed $x$, as in Step 3.)

One-wayness -- HOLDS (official solution, by reduction). Suppose $H$ were NOT one-way, i.e. there is an efficient function $g$ with $H(g(h)) = h$ for every digest $h$. Define $f(h) = \bigoplus \text{(the 256-bit blocks of } g(h) \text{)}$. Then by definition of $H$,
\[ \mathrm{SHA}(f(h)) = H(g(h)) = h \quad \text{for every } h, \]
so $f$ inverts SHA-2 on every output -- contradicting the assumed one-wayness of SHA. Hence $H$ is one-way.

exam_questions.answer: H is not collision resistant (H(x1||x2) = H(x2||x1), so weak and strong both fail), but it is one-way by reduction to SHA-2.

exam_questions.problem: Let $H(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} i \cdot x_i \bmod 2^{128}$ be a function that takes an input consisting of arbitrary $n$ blocks of 128 bits and returns the sum (in unsigned 128-bit arithmetic) of the product of the block content and block index. For example $H(x_1, x_2) = x_1 + 2 \cdot x_2 \bmod 2^{128}$ and $H(x_1, x_2, x_3) = x_1 + 2 \cdot x_2 + 3 \cdot x_3 \bmod 2^{128}$. Is $H$ a secure hash function? For each requirement of secure hash functions, disprove the requirement or argue why the requirement is met.

solution_steps.work: Definitions. \term{One-wayness}: given $h$, infeasible to find $x$ with $H(x) = h$. \term{Weak collision resistance}: given $x$, infeasible to find $y \neq x$ with $H(x) = H(y)$. \term{Strong collision resistance}: infeasible to find any $x \neq y$ with $H(x) = H(y)$.

Decompose: there is NO secure primitive here at all -- $H$ is a pure linear combiner over 128-bit blocks. So no reduction to a secure primitive is available; expect to break all three properties by direct algebra on the weighted sum. Useful handles: the coefficient of block 1 is $1$ (odd, hence invertible), and a block with value $0$ contributes nothing no matter its index.

One-wayness -- BROKEN (official solution: \q{just use $x := h$}). Given any target digest $h$ (a 128-bit value), take the SINGLE-block input $x = (x_1)$ with $x_1 = h$. Then
\[ H(x) = 1 \cdot x_1 \bmod 2^{128} = h, \]
a preimage produced with zero effort. The coefficient $1$ of the first block is what makes this trivial: block 1 passes straight through to the digest.

Weak collision resistance -- BROKEN (official solution). Given a fixed $x = (x_1, \dots, x_n)$, append one all-zero block: $y = (x_1, \dots, x_n, 0)$. The new block contributes $(n+1) \cdot 0 = 0$ to the sum, so
\[ H(y) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} i \cdot x_i + (n+1) \cdot 0 \;\bmod\, 2^{128} = H(x), \]
and $y \neq x$ since it has one more block.

Strong collision resistance -- BROKEN. The same zero-block trick already exhibits a colliding pair with both inputs chosen freely (pick any $x$, append a zero block), which by definition also wins the strong game. Equivalently, reorder-and-compensate: $x = (a, b)$ and $y = (b', a')$ with $a + 2b \equiv b' + 2a' \pmod{2^{128}}$ -- e.g. $x = (1, 1)$ gives sum $3$, and $y = (3)$ gives $1 \cdot 3 = 3$, so $H(1 \| 1) = H(3)$.

exam_questions.answer: H fails all three requirements: not one-way (x1 = h is a preimage), and not weakly or strongly collision resistant (appending a zero block yields a collision).
